endorsements.quote: For this reason, we advocate for a phased, dynamic process of implementation of LLMs that slowly tests the model in varied contexts of deployment before it is rolled out to more unpredictable ones, as we’ll elaborate in the next section.
A system validated for mild anxiety should not be extended to acute panic disorder or psychosis without specific testing.

Feedback should be gathered from both patients and clinicians, including traceable audit trails,[56]) such as systematic conversation logging especially with an eye on where adverse situations may have emerged.

In the first stage, the model is deployed in highly controlled, low-risk environments—the most obvious example here would be CBT support for patients with mild depression or anxiety—under close clinical supervision.
But this expansion remains conditional: deployment is authorised only where prior (use, context) pairs have been validated.
Most importantly, DCC recognises that certification is never finished.

unlisted_practices: Deploy LLM chatbots in psychiatry through staged, reversible, context-sensitive certification in which scope expands to new patient populations only after evidence of safety in adjacent populations.
Roll back or revoke certification of psychiatric LLM chatbots when new empirical findings reveal previously unrecognised risks.
Evaluate psychiatric LLM chatbot outputs for interpretive appropriateness to atypical users, not only truth or accuracy.
Use trained overseers capable of detecting context misalignment during limited rollouts of psychiatric chatbots.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual/governance framework paper proposing dynamic contextual certification (DCC) for deploying LLMs in psychiatry rather than an empirical study.
